content:
Slide 1 — Title
Redwood Private: VPC Terraform Modules (Alpha) — Pilot Customer Plan
Owner: Talia Benson (Program Mgmt)
Last updated: 2025-02-22

Speaker notes:
This deck is the execution plan for the alpha pilot of the AWS VPC Terraform modules that underpin Redwood Private (VPC) deployments. This is the cross-team plan used for internal readiness + customer delivery.


Slide 2 — What we are piloting (and why)
Goal
- Validate that reference Terraform modules reduce time-to-deploy and reduce support variance for Redwood Private (VPC).
- Validate secure-by-default posture (logging, endpoint hygiene, least-privilege networking patterns) with at least one “locked-down” enterprise environment.

In scope (alpha)
- AWS VPC baseline + subnet tiers
- NAT options (single vs per-AZ) OR private-only mode (no IGW/NAT)
- VPC endpoints: S3 gateway; ECR api/dkr; CloudWatch Logs; STS (and others if required by installer)
- Flow logs routing (CW Logs or S3)
- Wrapper module: redwood-private-vpc composing baseline + endpoints + SG
- Installer integration: consume TF outputs + networking preflight checks

Out of scope / explicitly not promising
- Multi-cloud parity
- Fully automated TGW / shared VPC governance across orgs (we will document integration points)
- Full custom NACL opinionation (we document guidance; SGs are the primary control surface)

Speaker notes:
We’ll treat the modules as reference/starting point. Alpha is about locking down the supported paths and removing sharp edges.


Slide 3 — Pilot customers (targets)
Customer A (codename: “NorthBridge”) — enterprise prospect (strict egress control)
- Constraints: prefer private endpoints; audit logging required; change control process
- Success indicator: deploy without public egress (or with explicit, controlled egress) and pass security review
- Source: HubSpot company-10492

Customer B (codename: “RedCedar”) — regulated customer starting in VPC, on-prem later
- Constraints: longer security signoff path; expects clear module versioning + rollback
- Success indicator: security signoff achieved with no material exceptions beyond alpha-defined list
- Source: HubSpot company-10511

Optional backup (if timing slips)
- Customer C: smaller AI-native team, existing VPC but fewer network constraints

Speaker notes:
We intentionally want one “hard mode” environment (private-only endpoints / no public egress). Backup is there to ensure we still validate install path even if enterprise change control delays.


Slide 4 — Entry criteria (before we start pilot execution)
Product readiness
- PM-611: Alpha definition agreed (scope + exit criteria + supported topologies)

Engineering readiness
- Wrapper module outputs stable enough for installer integration (subnet IDs, endpoint IDs/DNS, SG IDs)
- CI gates running (fmt/validate + tflint + checkov + integration apply test)

Security readiness
- Secure defaults review complete and documented (Confluence security review page)
- Known exceptions explicitly listed (with owner + expiration)

Docs readiness
- Quickstart is runnable end-to-end by someone not on the implementer team
- Troubleshooting guidance includes: endpoints, DNS, image pulls, and flow logs

Speaker notes:
We should not “discover” basics during pilot week 1. Pilot should validate real-world constraints and support model; not unblock missing fundamentals.


Slide 5 — Success metrics (quantitative)
Primary metrics (exit criteria candidates)
1) Deployment time reduction
- Baseline (current PS-led bespoke networking): 10–20 business days depending on env
- Target (with modules): <= 5 business days to a validated VPC foundation (not including customer procurement/change board)
- Measurement: calendar time + active engineer hours for Redwood PS/Infra

2) Installer success rate
- Target: 90% of installs succeed on first attempt (no Sev-2+ intervention)
- Measurement: number of apply/install attempts; number of manual workarounds

3) Support load / quality
- Target: 0 Sev-1 incidents attributable to module defaults during pilot
- Target: <= 2 Sev-2 support tickets across pilot attributable to modules (excluding AWS account issues)

4) Networking preflight signal quality
- Target: preflight catches at least 80% of misconfigurations observed in pilot before the installer proceeds
- Target: actionable error rate (support can map error -> doc/runbook) >= 90%

Secondary metrics
- Time to root cause for networking failures: <= 2 hours during business hours
- Documentation completeness score (internal rubric): >= 8/10 from PS + Support review

Speaker notes:
We’ll track both outcomes (time, success) and operational readiness (preflight + doc effectiveness). If we can’t support it predictably, we can’t scale.


Slide 6 — Success metrics (qualitative)
Customer feedback (required)
- “The Terraform modules made it clear what we needed to provide”
- “We could align our security team on endpoints/logging with minimal back-and-forth”
- “We understood what was supported vs not”

Internal feedback (required)
- Solutions/PS: confident delivering without bespoke networking per customer
- Infra/Security: confident the defaults are safe; exceptions process is workable
- Support: has a clear escalation path and runbooks

Speaker notes:
Qualitative feedback is part of exit criteria because we’ve historically lost time to unclear contracts + environmental ambiguity.


Slide 7 — Pilot phases + timeline (target)
Phase 0 — Prep (Week 0)
- Confirm customer selection + NDAs/security contacts
- Confirm target topology (public+private vs private-only)
- Confirm region(s) and AWS account model (single-account vs org-managed)

Phase 1 — Baseline deploy (Week 1)
- Terraform apply for VPC baseline + endpoints + SG baseline
- Validate outputs and run networking preflight checks

Phase 2 — Installer integration + install (Week 2)
- Provide installer config populated from module outputs
- Run install to green state
- Capture issues and categorize: docs gap / module bug / installer bug / customer env

Phase 3 — Hardening + re-run (Week 3)
- Incorporate fixes (patch releases)
- Re-apply / re-install where needed
- Update docs + runbooks

Phase 4 — Pilot closeout (Week 4)
- Retro + publish pilot report
- Go/No-Go recommendation for beta

Notes
- Enterprise customers may insert “security review” gates that extend calendar time; we measure active Redwood effort separately.

Speaker notes:
Timeline is intentionally short. If it runs longer, the closeout should still produce a clear beta readiness call.


Slide 8 — Detailed workplan (by week)
Week 0 (Prep)
- Kickoff call: confirm topology, DNS strategy, egress model, log sink requirements
- Share: Quickstart + architecture overview + required IAM permissions
- Create shared pilot channel + escalation contacts

Week 1 (Terraform)
- PS runs initial terraform plan with customer
- Apply with agreed tagging + logging settings
- Validate endpoints: ECR api/dkr, S3 gateway route tables, CloudWatch Logs, STS
- Validate DNS behavior (private DNS toggles) + resolver requirements

Week 2 (Installer)
- Generate installer networking config from outputs
- Run preflight checks; fix mismatches
- Install control plane + data plane components

Week 3 (Stabilization)
- Patch release window (1–2 days) for module/installer fixes
- Confirm idempotency: re-apply terraform is clean; re-run installer safe

Week 4 (Close)
- Capture metrics; write pilot report; decide beta backlog and release timeline

Speaker notes:
The focus is getting to a repeatable, supportable pattern. We will resist “one-off” customization unless it becomes a supported module input with guardrails.


Slide 9 — Roles and responsibilities (RACI-ish)
Program / orchestration
- DRI: Talia Benson
- Responsibilities: schedule, risk tracking, cross-team escalations, go/no-go meetings

Product
- DRI: Vivek Kulkarni
- Responsibilities: scope, supported topology decisions, alpha/beta gate criteria, customer comms alignment

Infra networking
- DRIs: Irene Choi (lead), Victor Alvarez (architect), Nina Petrova (review)
- Responsibilities: topology guardrails, endpoint/DNS patterns, review customer constraints, approve deviations

Security
- DRIs: Marcus Lin (approver), Kevin Osei (implementation guidance), Hanae Suzuki (KMS hooks guidance)
- Responsibilities: secure defaults sign-off, logging expectations, exceptions approval (time-bounded)

Platform / installer integration
- DRIs: Ethan Park (lead), Benji Okafor (contracts)
- Responsibilities: required outputs contract, preflight checks, installer error messaging, safe failure modes

Solutions / delivery
- DRIs: Markus Klein (stakeholder), Colin O'Donnell (pilot solutions lead), Bruno Silva (module implementer)
- Responsibilities: customer-facing deployment execution, capture feedback, validate docs are usable

Docs
- DRIs: Elliot Price (lead), Kira Thompson (writer)
- Responsibilities: quickstart + troubleshooting + versioning/rollback docs, publish/placement decisions

CI / quality gates
- DRI: Sahana Iyer
- Responsibilities: CI reliability, integration test flakes, pass/fail gating, suppression policy hygiene

Speaker notes:
If an issue is ambiguous (module vs installer vs env), PS owns driving to clarity; Platform/Infra own fixes in their domains. Program owns escalation and timeline.


Slide 10 — Customer touchpoints + comms
Standing meetings (recommended)
- 30 min weekly pilot sync (Redwood + customer)
- 15 min internal triage (daily during Week 1–2)

Channels
- Shared Slack Connect (if possible) OR email distro
- Internal: #eng-private-deployments (triage), #eng-infra (network review), #eng-security (signoff)

Artifacts to share with customer
- Architecture overview (VPC topology + required endpoints)
- Quickstart + tfvars examples for selected topology
- Installer networking prerequisites + preflight expectations
- Security posture summary (flow logs, logging sink, least privilege SG baseline)

Speaker notes:
We should set expectations early: “alpha = fast iteration”, but we will control changes through versions and communicate upgrade notes.


Slide 11 — Support and escalation model (pilot)
Severity definitions (pilot-specific)
- Sev-1: customer blocked, production impact, or security incident
- Sev-2: install blocked in pilot environment; workaround exists but needs Redwood intervention
- Sev-3: doc gaps, minor module issues, cosmetic/UX

Escalation path
1) Pilot channel triage (PS + Infra on point)
2) If installer-related: page Platform on-call (Ethan / Benji rotation)
3) If security concern: involve Marcus/Kevin immediately; stop-the-line if needed
4) If customer-facing comms needed: Vivek + Markus align response

On-call coverage expectation (pilot weeks 1–2)
- Business hours “rapid response” target: acknowledge within 30 minutes, next update within 2 hours
- After-hours: best effort unless Sev-1

Ticketing
- Every Sev-2+ issue gets a ticket (Jira Support or Linear) with:
  - customer impact
  - reproduction steps
  - logs/screenshots
  - decision: module change vs docs vs installer

Speaker notes:
We need repeatable support mechanisms before beta. Pilot is where we prove we can triage efficiently.


Slide 12 — Known risks + mitigations
Risk: Endpoint eventual consistency / race conditions during apply
- Mitigation: explicit depends_on ordering + retry guidance; CI integration tests across regions
- Reference: SUP-2204 + redwood-terraform PR-254

Risk: “No public egress” environments missing one endpoint (common)
- Mitigation: endpoint requirements matrix + installer preflight checks; docs with exact AWS services
- Reference: SUP-2197 and preflight runbook

Risk: Existing VPC adoption complexity (shared networking, TGW)
- Mitigation: explicitly supported “partial adoption mode” with guardrails; non-goals documented

Risk: Security review delays (customer change control)
- Mitigation: provide security summary + logging posture early; keep exception list tight and time-bounded

Risk: Module interface churn during alpha
- Mitigation: pin versions; publish upgrade notes; only patch releases during pilot unless absolutely required

Speaker notes:
Most risk is around “edge enterprise reality”. The mitigations are documentation, strong validation, and predictable change management.


Slide 13 — Go/No-Go gates
Gate A — Start pilot (end of Week 0)
- Docs quickstart passes internal dry-run
- CI gates green including integration apply
- Security signoff complete OR documented, approved exceptions

Gate B — Declare pilot success (end of Week 3/4)
- At least one customer environment deployed and installer reaches green state
- Success metrics hit (or variance explained with corrective plan)
- Support runbooks updated with issues encountered

Gate C — Recommend beta
- Stable module interfaces + outputs contract for installer
- Clear supported topology matrix + explicit non-supported patterns
- Versioning + rollback guidance complete and reviewed

Speaker notes:
If we miss a gate, we should convert to a clear “pilot extended” plan with a new date and explicit deltas—not drift indefinitely.


Slide 14 — Data to collect during pilot (for postmortem + ROI)
Operational metrics
- # terraform apply attempts; # failures; root causes
- # installer runs; # preflight failures; # installer failures; root causes
- Time to first successful apply; time to first successful install

Support metrics
- # tickets by severity; time to acknowledge; time to resolution
- # escalations to infra/security/platform

Customer environment details (non-sensitive summary)
- Region, egress model, DNS model, log sink choice
- Existing VPC vs net-new VPC

Deliverables (end of pilot)
- Pilot report (2–4 pages) with: metrics, issues, fixes shipped, beta backlog

Speaker notes:
We need consistent data collection or we’ll argue feelings. Program will run a simple tracker and assign owners to fill it out weekly.


Slide 15 — Deliverables checklist (what “done” looks like)
Engineering
- Wrapper module produces a stable set of outputs consumed by installer
- Integration tests cover selected topology (public+private or private-only)
- Known failure modes have deterministic error messages (preflight)

Security
- Flow logs options documented (CW vs S3), with retention recommendations
- Secure defaults documented; exception list expires

Docs
- Quickstart with tfvars examples for both:
  - minimal baseline
  - enterprise locked-down (private-only endpoints/no public egress)
- Troubleshooting page includes:
  - ECR pulls fail (missing endpoints)
  - S3 access missing route table association
  - STS missing causes auth failures
  - DNS resolver requirements for private DNS

Support readiness
- Escalation path + on-call expectations in writing
- Runbook links embedded in installer errors where possible

Speaker notes:
This is the real output of the pilot: not just “it worked once” but “we can repeat it and support it.”


Slide 16 — Open questions / decisions needed (as of 2025-02-22)
1) Endpoint set finalization
- Is STS required in all “no public egress” deployments? (Recent on-call thread suggests yes; needs formalization.)

2) DNS resolver expectations
- When private DNS is enabled for interface endpoints, what do we require from customer DNS (Route53 resolver, forwarders)?

3) NAT strategy default
- Default to single NAT for cost; allow per-AZ NAT for resiliency. Need crisp guidance on when to choose which.

4) Logging defaults
- Default Flow Logs to CloudWatch with 14 days retention? Or S3 preferred for enterprises?

5) Existing VPC adoption boundaries
- What do we support in alpha vs defer to beta? (TGW + shared route tables currently high variance.)

Owners
- Irene/Victor: #1, #3, #5
- Ethan/Benji: #2 (preflight) + output contracts
- Marcus/Kevin: #4 + secure defaults language

Speaker notes:
We can proceed with pilot while these are being resolved, but we should avoid promising outcomes that depend on unsettled decisions.
